findings.title: Unverified JWT Token Acceptance - Authentication Bypass
findings.impact: An attacker can craft arbitrary JWT tokens with any claims (user ID, role, tenant) without a valid signature. The jwt.decode() function only decodes the payload without verification, allowing complete authentication bypass. Any attacker can impersonate any user.
findings.evidence: jwt.decode(bearer) is called without jwt.verify(). The function returns decoded claims without signature validation. Both currentUser() and tagRequest() use this vulnerable pattern.
findings.recommendation: Replace jwt.decode() with jwt.verify() using a shared secret or public key. Example: jwt.verify(bearer, SECRET, {algorithms: ['HS256']}) or jwt.verify(bearer, PUBLIC_KEY, {algorithms: ['RS256']}).

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in Invoice Note Rendering
findings.impact: User-controlled invoice notes are directly embedded into HTML without escaping. An attacker can inject malicious JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser when viewing the invoice, potentially stealing session cookies, performing unauthorized actions, or defacing the page.
findings.evidence:
invoiceNote() function at line 4 returns `
${note}
` without calling escapeHtml(note). The note parameter comes directly from user input. Compare with customerName() on line 8 which correctly uses escapeHtml().
findings.recommendation:
Call escapeHtml() on the note parameter: return `
${escapeHtml(note)}
`;. This will properly escape HTML entities in user input.

findings.title: SQL Injection via ORDER BY Parameter
findings.impact: The 'order' query parameter is directly interpolated into the SQL query without parameterization or validation. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL code by crafting a malicious 'order' parameter, allowing data exfiltration, modification, or deletion from the database.
findings.evidence: Line 16: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, ...). The 'order' variable comes from req.query.order with only a default fallback. Contrast with /payments endpoint (line 23) which uses an explicit whitelist SORTABLE[req.query.sort].
findings.recommendation: Implement a whitelist of allowed column names: const ALLOWED_ORDERS = {created_at: 'created_at', amount: 'total_cents'}; const order = ALLOWED_ORDERS[req.query.order] || 'created_at';. Then use this validated value in the query.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in Logo Fetching
findings.impact: The fetchLogo() function fetches arbitrary URLs without validation. An attacker can cause the server to make requests to internal addresses (localhost:6379 for Redis, 169.254.169.254 for AWS metadata, internal databases) or arbitrary external servers, potentially exposing internal data or enabling attack pivots.
findings.evidence: fetchLogo() at line 5 accepts any URL and calls fetch(url) with only redirect: 'follow'. No hostname validation occurs. Contrast with fetchAsset() which has whitelist validation on line 11.
findings.recommendation: Add hostname validation before fetching. Use a whitelist of allowed domains or implement URL parsing to block internal/private IP ranges: const url = new URL(logoUrl); const blocked = ['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '0.0.0.0', '169.254.169.254', /^192\.168/, /^10\./, /^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])/]; if (blocked.some(...)) throw new Error('host not allowed');.

findings.title: Unauthorized Access to Invoice Data - Missing Owner Verification
findings.impact: The /invoices/:id endpoint returns invoice data without verifying ownership. An attacker can access any invoice by guessing or enumerating invoice IDs, exposing sensitive billing information belonging to other users. This is a direct authorization bypass.
findings.evidence: Line 8: const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]). This filters only by id, not by owner_id. Contrast with /receipts/:id at lines 12-17 which correctly filters by both id AND owner_id: WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2.
findings.recommendation: Add owner verification: const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2', [req.params.id, req.user.id]); Also verify req.user exists with authentication middleware.

findings.title: Missing Authentication Middleware Enforcement
findings.impact: Routes access req.user.id without explicit authentication middleware enforcement. If the middleware is misconfigured or missing, req.user could be undefined, causing requests to use NULL owner_id filters or behave unexpectedly. Additionally, the /invoices/:id endpoint has no owner check even with authentication.
findings.evidence: Routes like /receipts/:id (line 12), /invoices (line 19), /payments (line 27) all access req.user.id without a preceding middleware that validates the JWT and sets req.user. The currentUser() function can return {id: undefined} if no valid Bearer token is provided.
findings.recommendation: Add authentication middleware before all protected routes: router.use((req, res, next) => {const user = currentUser(req); if (!user.id) return res.status(401).json({error: 'Unauthorized'}); req.user = user; next();}). Also ensure /invoices/:id has owner verification as per F-005.

findings.title: Open Redirect / Unvalidated Redirect in SSRF
findings.impact: The fetchLogo() function uses redirect: 'follow' allowing HTTP redirects. An attacker could exploit a third-party's open redirect to bypass hostname validation and trigger SSRF to internal addresses. A malicious host could redirect to localhost, internal IP addresses, or other sensitive services.
findings.evidence: Line 6: await fetch(url, { redirect: 'follow' }) allows following redirects. This is set to 'error' in fetchAsset() on line 14, which is more restrictive. With redirect: 'follow', even if initial validation existed, the server could be redirected to internal addresses.
findings.recommendation: Use redirect: 'error' to disallow redirects: fetch(url, { redirect: 'error' }). This prevents attackers from using intermediate open redirects to bypass SSRF protections.
